items.reason: Source: "Stubb heeded not the mumblings of the banquet that was going on so nigh him". Candidate "paid no attention to the feast being held so close to him" drops "mumblings", the sound image that pairs with "the smacking of his own epicurean lips" in the same sentence and echoes "Mingling their mumblings" in 64.7.
items.new: But as yet Stubb paid no attention to the mumblings of the banquet going on so close to him, any more than the sharks noticed the smacking of his own gourmet lips.

items.reason: Source: "here interposed Stubb, accompanying the word with a sudden slap on the shoulder". Candidate "slapping him on the shoulder" loses "sudden" (the abruptness is the comic beat of Stubb's interruption).
items.new: "Cook," Stubb cut in here, with a sudden slap on the shoulder, "Cook! Why, damn your eyes, you mustn't swear that way when you're preaching. That's no way to convert sinners, cook!"

items.reason: Source: "Talk to 'em gentlemanly." (= speak in a gentlemanly way). Candidate "Talk to them like gentlemen" reads as 'address them as if they were gentlemen', a different instruction. Minimal fix keeps the manner on the speaker.
items.new: "Cook," cried Stubb, grabbing him by the collar, "I won't have that swearing. Talk to them like a gentleman."

items.reason: Open question answered. Source: "de dam willains will keep a scougin' and slappin' each oder". "scougin'" is best read as Fleece's form of "scrougin'" (scrouge = crowd, squeeze, jostle), the same word he used two paragraphs earlier (64.23 "dat can't get into de scrouge", rendered "crush"); the reciprocal "each oder" and the scene (sharks crowding the carcass) fit. The repair's "a-scourgin'" asserts whipping/lashing, a sense the text does not support. Use a plain, light-dialect jostling verb consistent with 64.23.
items.new: "No use goin' on; de damn villains will keep a-jostlin' and slappin' each other, Massa Stubb; dey don't hear one word; no use a-preachin' to such damn gluttons as you call 'em, till dere bellies is full, and dere bellies is bottomless; and when dey do get 'em full, dey won't hear you den; for den dey sink in de sea, go fast to sleep on de coral, and can't hear nothin' at all, no more, for ever and ever."

items.reason: Source: "make a bow before you go". Candidate "Take a bow" is modern idiom for accepting applause, not bowing to Stubb as a dismissal courtesy. Keep "Make a bow".
items.new: "Cook, give me cutlets for supper tomorrow night during the mid-watch. Do you hear? Away you sail, then. — Wait! Stop! Make a bow before you go. — Hold on! Whale-balls for breakfast — don't forget."
